tldr: WorldMirror is an agentic real-to-sim framework where an autonomous coding agent orchestrates 3D generative tools and refines an executable world program via verification feedback, turning in-the-wild robot manipulation videos and joint trajectories into interactive digital twins that can directly replay recorded motions without retargeting.
hero_caption: Comparison between an existing general-purpose agent (GPT-6 Astra) and WorldMirror. While GPT-6 Astra excels at spatial layout reasoning, it struggles with appearance fidelity and contact physics. In contrast, WorldMirror achieves both photorealistic appearance and physically consistent collision geometry.
overview:
Training general-purpose robot policies requires diverse real-world interaction data, yet physical robot data collection and testing remain prohibitively expensive. Simulation-based training (Sim-to-Real / Real-to-Sim) offers a promising alternative, but traditional workflows require labor-intensive manual scene authoring and task specification, which severely limits scalability. Meanwhile, open-source datasets of in-the-wild manipulation demonstrations contain vast amounts of realistic interactions. However, simply turning images into 3D meshes cannot produce physically consistent environments where robots can reliably contact and manipulate objects.

To solve this, the authors introduce WorldMirror, which formulates real-to-sim construction as the iterative refinement of an executable world program. A coding agent decomposes the observed scene, invokes specialized 3D generation and calibration tools, and refines the program using verification feedback from the simulator. Furthermore, by anchoring static background context, support surfaces, interactive objects, and the robot base into a unified coordinate system relative to the camera pose, recorded joint trajectories can be directly replayed in simulation without any modifications.

Evaluations on the large-scale real-world DROID dataset demonstrate that WorldMirror achieves high visual fidelity and precise geometric alignment compared to open-source baselines and GPT-6 Astra. Notably, in direct trajectory replay, WorldMirror achieved a 100% success rate—compared to only 40% for GPT-6 Astra—highlighting its superior physical consistency.
contributions: Proposed WorldMirror, an agentic real-to-sim framework that builds interactive digital twins from real-world videos via adaptive tool orchestration and verification-driven iterative refinement of an executable world program.

Introduced a camera-pose-anchored scene representation that unifies static context, support geometry, and interactive assets, enabling direct replay of real robot joint trajectories without retargeting.
Demonstrated high visual fidelity, precise geometric layout accuracy, and physical interaction fidelity (100% replay success rate) on real-world manipulation sequences from the DROID dataset.

sections.heading: Can we automatically turn in-the-wild robot videos into interactive simulators?
sections.summary: Scaling robot learning across diverse real-world environments requires simulation, but building scenes manually is impractical. WorldMirror autonomously generates interactive digital twins from in-the-wild robot manipulation videos.
sections.details:
Scaling general-purpose robot policies requires data covering diverse real-world scenarios. However, collecting demonstrations and evaluating policies on real hardware is both expensive and tedious. While simulation provides an attractive alternative, doing so requires matching not only visual appearance, but also object placement, camera views, robot placement, and contact physics with exceptional precision.

A minor scale mismatch or subtle collision penetration can completely alter task outcomes in simulation. Conventional feedforward (single-pass) reconstruction methods struggle to simultaneously satisfy these tightly coupled visual, geometric, and physical constraints. Moreover, different errors demand fundamentally different remedies: a misaligned object requires layout optimization, whereas a missing object demands re-segmentation.

This insight highlights the necessity of an agentic world modeling approach: rather than following a rigid tool-calling sequence, an agent should autonomously select corrective actions based on the current world state and verification feedback. To realize this, the authors developed WorldMirror, where a coding agent orchestrates specialized tools to iteratively refine an executable world program.

sections.heading: How does it compare to prior work: moving from feedforward reconstruction to agentic, verification-driven modeling
sections.summary: The paper contextualizes WorldMirror relative to recent progress in real-to-sim generation, agentic 3D modeling, and robot learning benchmarks.
sections.details:
### Real-to-Sim Environment Construction
Many reconstruction approaches have been explored, such as RialTo using real scene scans, RoLA reconstructing from a single image, and PolaRiS leveraging video scans. More recent methods, including SimFoundry, RoboSnap, and TwinAligner, integrate geometric alignment and physics parameter estimation. WorldMirror advances this line of work by managing the entire scene as an executable program and supporting component-level revision guided by verification feedback.

### Agentic 3D Modeling
Research leveraging multimodal agents to build and manipulate 3D scenes is expanding rapidly. Alongside general-purpose agents like GPT-6 Astra, specialized frameworks like Articraft, SAGE, and LiteReality combine dedicated tools with self-critique loops. In particular, Agentic Real2Sim incorporates simulator refinement. WorldMirror distinguishes itself by structuring the world state inside a shared memory, using a hierarchical router to coordinate specialized agents, and employing a unified camera-anchored coordinate system that enables direct trajectory replay.

### Simulators for Robot Learning
Platforms such as RLBench, robosuite, ManiSkill, SIMPLER, and RoboTwin have established diverse environments for policy training. WorldMirror functions as an automated engine that bridges raw, in-the-wild demonstration datasets to these simulation platforms.

sections.heading: How WorldMirror works: four specialized agents and a camera-pose-anchored coordinate system
sections.summary: WorldMirror defines the simulation environment as an executable program, where a router agent coordinates four specialized sub-agents and a skill library. A camera-anchored frame enables direct replay of recorded joint trajectories.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Problem Formulation
The goal is to formalize a process $\mathcal{A}$ that converts a real-world RGB demonstration $\mathcal{V}$ and robot joint trajectory $\mathcal{T}$ into an interactive digital twin. The resulting simulation must preserve visual appearance, maintain editable interactive objects (with geometric and physical fidelity), and share a coordinate frame that permits direct trajectory replay without motion replanning.

### 3.2 Structured World State Memory
All agents share a structured world state memory. At step $t$, the confirmed state comprises static context $\mathcal{S}_t$, interactive objects $\mathcal{O}_t$, geometric and spatial relations $\mathcal{R}_t$, and verification/failure feedback $\mathcal{F}_t$. Candidate updates proposed by specialized agents are only committed to memory once they pass validation checks. When a check fails, typed error feedback is logged, and dependent downstream components are invalidated for re-estimation.

### 3.3 Agentic World Construction
The overall execution flow is orchestrated by a Router Agent. The router manages state transitions along an execution graph (scene prep → calibration → support surface estimation → object generation → layout → robot alignment → trajectory replay). Concrete tasks are delegated to four specialized sub-agents through an "Agent-as-Tool" paradigm:
- Reconstruction Agent: Generates the static background (Gaussian representation), support geometry, and interactive 3D assets using tools like Meshy and Articraft.
- Calibration Agent: Estimates camera extrinsic parameters by combining DINOv2 dense correspondences and LSD line-segment matching.
- Layout Agent: Optimizes 6-DoF object poses and scales to align with visual masks and contours.
- Replay Agent: Executes joint trajectories and validates contacts inside Isaac Sim.

### 3.4 Verification-Driven Refinement
At each pipeline stage, candidates are evaluated across visual, spatial, and physical criteria. If an inconsistency is detected, the router receives the failure diagnosis along with a rollback target, backtracking along the dependency graph to apply targeted refinements.

### 3.5 Camera-Pose-Anchored Coordinate Representation
Let $T_{C \to W}$ denote the transformation matrix from the calibrated camera frame $C$ to the unified world frame $W$. Any point $P^C$ in the camera frame is mapped to the world frame via $P^W = T_{C \to W} P^C$. By anchoring the relative transformation between the camera and the robot base from the real demonstration into this unified frame, the recorded joint trajectory can be directly replayed in simulation without any alterations.

captions.F2: Overall architecture of WorldMirror. The workspace on the left maintains the structured world state, while the top-center Router directs four specialized sub-agents (Reconstruction, Calibration, Layout, and Replay). Agents call tools from a library, and when the verification module (bottom right) flags a failure, the pipeline automatically rolls back to the appropriate previous step for refinement.

sections.heading: 100% trajectory replay: rigorous evaluation of visual realism and physical validity
sections.summary: Evaluations on the real-world DROID dataset demonstrate that WorldMirror outperforms open-source baselines and GPT-6 Astra in visual fidelity and physical consistency, achieving a 100% success rate on direct trajectory replay.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Experimental Setup
The authors selected 10 challenging manipulation scenes from the real-world DROID dataset. WorldMirror is compared against prior real-to-sim methods (RoLA, RoboSnap, SimFoundry) and the large multimodal agent GPT-6 Astra. Evaluation metrics span visual fidelity (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, DISTS), spatial layout fidelity (mask IoU, position error, relative vector and distance errors), and replay fidelity (displacement error, contact F1-score, and replay success rate).

### 4.2 Appearance Reconstruction
Comparing first-frame simulation renderings against real camera views, WorldMirror achieved the best scores across perceptual similarity metrics LPIPS and DISTS (where lower is better). As shown in Figure F3, visual textures of background office desks and kitchen sinks are naturally restored.

### 4.3 Spatial Geometry and Layout Preservation
Spatial layout accuracy was evaluated across 17 interactive objects and 8 object pairs. WorldMirror significantly outperformed all open-source baselines across all metrics. While GPT-6 Astra showed slightly higher mask IoU and lower absolute position error in select cases, WorldMirror achieved the lowest relative distance error, demonstrating superior preservation of inter-object spatial relationships.

### 4.4 Trajectory Replay and Physical Interaction
Real joint trajectories were directly streamed into Isaac Sim. GPT-6 Astra suffered from inaccurate object shapes and misaligned support surfaces, causing the gripper to miss or drop objects and yielding only a 40% replay success rate. In contrast, WorldMirror achieved a higher contact F1-score and achieved a 100% replay success rate across all evaluated demonstrations (Table 4).

### 4.5 Ablation Studies
Ablations comparing verification feedback strategies revealed that single-pass reconstruction (One-pass) or blind retry loops (Fixed Iterative) frequently caused the gripper to miss contacts entirely, leaving objects stationary (Figure F5). Only Full WorldMirror, guided by targeted diagnostic feedback, reliably completed the manipulation. Additionally, removing adaptive routing drastically worsened trajectory tracking errors, confirming that rigid pipelines cannot handle varied real-world failures.

Without feedback (left), misaligned object placement and contacts leave the object stationary; incorporating error diagnosis and iterative rollbacks (right) allows the robot to successfully place the object at the target location.

sections.heading: Takeaways and future directions: unlocking real-world video archives for simulation learning
sections.summary: WorldMirror demonstrates that interactive digital twins can be faithfully constructed from in-the-wild robot videos, underscoring the vital need to tightly integrate visual reconstruction with physics verification.
sections.details:
By uniting structured world state memory, specialized sub-agent orchestration, and verification-driven iterative refinement, WorldMirror successfully generates high-fidelity interactive environments from uncurated real-world demonstrations. The experiments prove that visual matching alone is insufficient: closing the loop with physical contact verification and trajectory-level replay feedback is essential.

Current limitations include evaluating only on a subset of demonstrations from the DROID dataset, without downstream policy training via reinforcement or imitation learning, nor deployment back onto physical robots (Sim-to-Real). Furthermore, reconstruction quality remains bounded by the capabilities of underlying 3D generative backends and physics simulation engines. Future work will focus on expanding to more diverse manipulation tasks and validating large-scale policy training within the generated digital twins.

takeaways: Representing the world as an executable program and backtracking to localized error sources via verification feedback is far more effective for ensuring physical consistency than relying on single-pass generative models.

Anchoring static context, support surfaces, dynamic objects, and the robot base to the camera frame allows recorded real-world joint trajectories to be directly replayed with 100% fidelity without inverse kinematics or replanning.
High visual fidelity (LPIPS/DISTS) and physically valid contact geometry must be solved together; using simulation task outcome as an agent feedback signal points to a promising new paradigm.
limitations: Evaluations are limited to 10 scenes and specific tasks from the DROID dataset; scalability to highly complex geometries or deformable objects has not been verified.
The framework has not yet been demonstrated in a complete closed loop: training policies inside the reconstructed worlds and deploying them back to real hardware (Sim-to-Real-to-Sim).
Overall reconstruction quality is ultimately constrained by the performance ceilings of the underlying 3D generative backends (e.g., Meshy, Articraft) and physics engine (Isaac Sim).
